title: Thirty-year trends gave no clear common gain in annual cherry bloom forecasts at three sites in 1981-2025
abstract: We tested whether a trend from the prior 30 years reduced cherry bloom forecast error relative to the mean of the same years. We used 75 annual records at each of Kyoto, Liestal and Washington. Each forecast used only earlier records. Tests covered 1981-2002 and 2003-2025. Changes in mean absolute error ranged from -1.85 to +0.46 days. All six 95 percent block intervals included zero. All six intervals adjusted for multiple tests also included zero. A 20-year window changed some signs and gave no clear common gain. The rolling mean had lower error than a fixed 1951-1980 mean in all six samples. This descriptive result separates an updated baseline from an added trend. Fixed sites and complete years reduce changes in site coverage. Changes in trees, bloom rules and observation effort remain possible. The test uses revised historical records and is not a trial of forecasts issued in real time. It does not measure a causal climate effect, pollution or species loss. The package includes source hashes, annual losses, code, checks and a figure.

display.caption: Forecast error from earlier records only. Left: trend minus rolling-mean absolute error. Thick bars are 95 percent block intervals; thin bars are six-test adjusted intervals. Negative values favor the trend. Right: fixed mean, rolling mean and trend errors. Upper rows are 1981-2002; lower rows are 2003-2025.

citations.reason: Prior ENSO forecast test uses the same biological archive. Our test compares forecast baselines without climate predictors.
Prior local-temperature forecast test uses a trend baseline. Our test asks whether a trend improves on an updated mean.
Prior annual-agreement study informed the fixed-site scope. Records overlap; this is not independent validation of these records.
